titre: AI-driven radiopharmaceutical dosimetry optimization for theranostics: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
revue: Revista espanola de medicina nuclear e imagen molecular
resume: Introduction Personalised radioligand therapy (RLT) depends on accurate absorbed-dose estimation. Standard dosimetry requires multiple post-therapy single-photon emission computed tomography/computed tomography (SPECT/CT) acquisitions, imposing logistical burdens. Machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) have been proposed to streamline organ segmentation, generate synthetic imaging timepoints, and predict patient-specific doses. We evaluated the performance, methodological quality, and translational readiness of artificial intelligence (AI)-driven dosimetry in the clinical theranostics literature. Methods In this systematic review and meta-analysis, we searched PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and regional databases (Jan 1, 2014, to March 1, 2025). Studies applying AI to dosimetry in human RLT recipients were eligible. Two reviewers screened and extracted data. Risk of bias was assessed with the Prediction model Risk Of Bias ASsessment Tool (PROBAST) and the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies-2 (QUADAS-2). Meta-analyses of organ segmentation (Dice similarity coefficient [DSC]) and dose prediction (concordance correlation coefficient [CCC]) used restricted maximum-likelihood (REML) random-effects models restricted to studies with independent validation sets. Prospero CRD420261349805 (https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/display_record.php?RecordID=1349805). Results 58 studies met inclusion criteria covering 1847 patients (1523 [82%] male, 324 [18%] female). 23 studies with independent validation were eligible for meta-analysis. Pooled DSC was 0·87 (95% CI 0·83-0·90; 16 studies). Pooled voxel dosimetry relative absolute error (RAE) was 6·1% (4·6-8·1%; 12 studies). Pretherapy kidney dose prediction yielded pooled CCC 0·79 (0·72-0·85; 8 studies). PROBAST identified high risk of bias in 71% of prediction studies. Reducing timepoints from ≥3 to 1-2 scans increased RAE by 8·2 percentage points (5·1-11·4). AI reduced median processing time from 180 to 25 minutes. Conclusions On independent validation data, AI-driven dosimetry shows promising accuracy for organ-level dose estimation and substantially reduces processing time. However, the evidence base remains immature: 71% of prediction studies carry high risk of bias, only four studies report external validation, and most pooled outcomes were graded as low or very low certainty. External multicentre validation and prospective randomised trials comparing AI-guided against fixed-activity RLT are needed before clinical adoption. Current evidence primarily demonstrates technical feasibility rather than proven clinical utility.

titre: AI Predictive Models for Discharge Disposition in Patients Following Primary Total Knee Arthroplasty: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
auteurs: Xie D, Chen R, Yue C, Liu X, Cao G, Jiao R.
types: meta-analysis systematic review review journal article
resume: Background Although a growing number of AI-based predictive models for discharge disposition in patients following primary total knee arthroplasty (TKA) have been constructed, their performance, quality, and applicability remain unclear. Objective This study aimed to evaluate the performance, quality, and applicability of published AI-based predictive models for discharge disposition in patients following primary TKA. Methods PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, the Cochrane Library, Scopus, China National Knowledge Infrastructure, Wanfang Database, China Science and Technology Journal Database, and SinoMed Database were searched from inception to May 26, 2025. We included original studies that developed AI-based predictive models for discharge disposition in adult patients (age ≥18 years) undergoing primary TKA. Studies involving simultaneous bilateral or revision TKA or those that did not develop a predictive model were excluded. Risk of bias and reporting quality were assessed using the PROBAST+AI (Prediction Model Risk of Bias Assessment Tool+AI) and TRIPOD+AI (Transparent Reporting of a Multivariable Prediction Model for Individual Prognosis or Diagnosis+AI), respectively. Pooled area under the curve values and 95% CIs were estimated using a DerSimonian-Laird random-effects model with the Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman adjustment. Heterogeneity was assessed using the Cochran Q test and I ² statistic. Subgroup analyses were conducted according to algorithm type, categorized as machine learning (ML)-based and deep learning (DL)-based models. Results A total of 5 retrospective studies from the United States involving 4 ML-based models and 1 DL-based model were included, with sample sizes ranging from 175,042 to 434,550 patients. Age and sex were the most frequently used predictors. All included studies were rated as having a high risk of bias according to the PROBAST+AI checklist. The pooled area under the curve was 0.75 (95% CI 0.67-0.82; I ²=99.9%; P I ²=99.8%; P P >.05). Conclusions AI-based predictive models for discharge disposition following primary TKA demonstrate a certain level of discriminative performance. However, the current evidence is limited, as all included studies were at high risk of bias and showed a high degree of heterogeneity. In addition, all included studies were conducted in the United States, which may limit the generalizability of these findings to other health care settings. Future studies should follow PROBAST+AI and TRIPOD+AI checklists while developing and validating models across different countries and health care systems.

titre: External validation of an artificial intelligence-based ECG algorithm for the early diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction: a prospective diagnostic cohort study.
auteurs: Champetier A, Lee MS, Lopez-Ayala P, Jo YY, Boeddinghaus J, Koechlin L, Bima P, Crisanti L, Zimmermann T, Kim K, Kim KS, Yoon S, Kaplan E, Gualandro DM, Recuenco LH, Huré G, Tsao TY, Nani M, Lee HS, K
resume: Background A novel artificial intelligence-based electrocardiogram (AI-ECG) model (AiTiA MI v2.00.00) for the early diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction (AMI) was developed using data from Korean patients. Its performance in a European population remains unknown. Methods Patients presenting to the emergency department (ED) with suspected AMI were enrolled in two prospective European cohorts (APACE & APACE-Light; ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT00470587). The primary outcome was AMI, centrally adjudicated according to the fourth Universal Definition of MI. The AI-ECG model was applied to 12-lead ECGs recorded at ED presentation. Its diagnostic performance for AMI was directly compared to that of the BASEL score, high-sensitivity cardiac troponin T (hs-cTnT), the recalibrated HEART score (all at ED presentation), and integrated physician judgment at 90 min, with the last two only available in APACE. Predefined AI-ECG triage thresholds for early rule-out and rule-in of AMI were also evaluated. Findings Among 12,630 patients with an available digital 12-lead ECG (5047 in APACE and 7583 in APACE-Light), adjudicated AMI was diagnosed in 19% (968/5047) and 18% (1386/7583) of patients, respectively. In patients with hs-cTnT at presentation (n = 5031 and n = 7565), the AI-ECG model showed good diagnostic performance for AMI with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.78 (95% CI: 0.77-0.80) and 0.84 (0.83-0.85) and an area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) of 0.56 (0.53-0.59) and 0.65 (0.62-0.67). Its discrimination was inferior to hs-cTnT (AUC 0.94 [0.93-0.95] and 0.93 [0.92-0.94]). The AI-ECG model provided some incremental diagnostic value when combined with hs-cTnT (AUC 0.95 [0.94-0.96] and 0.95 [0.94-0.95], p Interpretation AI-ECG showed high, but not very high, diagnostic accuracy for AMI. As a diagnosis of AMI is unlikely to be ruled out on ECG alone, combining AI-ECG with hs-cTnT may improve decision making in the ED, warranting prospective studies. titre: Medical Interview Performance Using an AI-Based Standardized Patient vs a Human Standardized Patient: Randomized Crossover Trial.
auteurs: Yanagita Y, Yokokawa D, Fukuzawa F, Ihara S, Yoshida R, Sato R, Uehara T.
resume: Background In Japan, standardized patients (SPs) have traditionally been recruited to teach medical interview competencies. Recent advances in large language models have enabled increasingly natural conversational interactions, raising the possibility of using AI-based SPs (AI-SPs) for medical interview training. However, medical interview performance during interactions with AI-SPs compared with human SPs remains insufficiently understood. Objective This randomized single-center crossover trial aimed to compare medical interview performance and learner-reported experiences between encounters with a large language model-based AI-SP and a human SP. Methods Participants were fifth-year medical students undertaking clinical clerkships at Chiba University Hospital. The AI-SP was a text-based simulated patient implemented using GPT-4o. Participants were randomized to AI-SP followed by human SP, or the reverse. A washout period of at least 3 days was set between conditions. Each participant completed 2 cases, depression and appendicitis, in both conditions. For the AI-SP interviews, chat logs were retained, and a physician provided feedback after completion of the 2 cases. Human SP interviews were video recorded, and the physician portraying the SP provided feedback immediately after each interview. Medical interview performance was assessed using selected items from the Mini-Clinical Evaluation Exercise (Mini-CEX), with ratings performed independently by 2 general medicine specialists. Participants completed a self-rated questionnaire (7-point Likert-type scale) regarding learning satisfaction, perceived rapport formation, and active engagement in history taking. Results Forty-eight participants were analyzed. The Mini-CEX-based mean total score was significantly higher for the human SP than for the AI-SP (23.9, SD 1.7 vs 22.7, SD 1.7, respectively; mean difference 1.24; t 47 =3.7; P=.001). Scores for history taking and overall clinical competence were higher in the human SP condition. Interrater reliability (intraclass correlation coefficient of 2,1) was 0.76 (95% CI 0.66-0.83). No significant differences were found between conditions for learning satisfaction (human SP: mean 5.9, SD 1.1; AI-SP: mean 6.0, SD 0.8) or perceived rapport formation (human SP: mean 5.4, SD 1.3; AI-SP: mean 5.3, SD 1.3). Active engagement in history taking was significantly higher in the AI-SP condition (human SP: mean 5.8, SD 1.1; AI-SP: mean 6.2, SD 0.7; t 47 =2.7; P=.009). Conclusions Medical interview performance differed between the 2 SP conditions, with higher history taking and overall clinical competence scores in the human SP condition. The text-based nature of the AI-SP and the absence of nonverbal cues may have contributed to these differences. Although no significant differences between conditions were observed in most other assessment outcomes, learning satisfaction, or perceived rapport, self-rated active engagement in history taking was higher with the AI-SP condition. AI-SPs may offer a complementary modality for medical interview practice; however, this study assessed performance during simulated encounters rather than subsequent learning gains or performance with real patients. Trial registration UMIN Clinical Trials Registry UMIN000056228; https://center6.umin.ac.jp/cgi-open-bin/ctr_e/ctr_view.cgi?recptno=R000064153.

titre: Artificial intelligence-enabled interventions for smoking cessation: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.
auteurs: Adebisi YA, Alhur AA, Ogunkola IO, Olaoye DQ, Ong CJN, Iyagbaye E, Lucero-Prisno Iii DE.
resume: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in digital smoking-cessation tools, but whether AI-enabled personalisation improves abstinence, and whether any benefit reflects the AI component rather than digital support more broadly, remain uncertain. Objective To systematically review and meta-analyse randomised controlled trials (RCTs) of AI-enabled smoking-cessation interventions using an explicit operational framework that distinguished learning, inference and substantive language-understanding components from conventional fixed-rule automation. Methods PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus and the Web of Science Core Collection were searched from inception to 7 August 2026 without language, date, publication-status or study-design filters; Cochrane CENTRAL, ClinicalTrials.gov and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform were searched, and backward and forward citation searching was undertaken, on 21 October 2026. Eligible studies were RCTs in adults who smoked combustible cigarettes in which an AI-enabled component materially generated, selected, personalised, adapted, predicted, recommended or timed cessation support. Two reviewers independently screened records, extracted data and assessed risk of bias using RoB 2; disagreements were resolved by a third reviewer. Risk ratios (RRs) were pooled using random-effects restricted maximum likelihood models with Knapp-Hartung adjustment, separately for abstinence at the longest follow-up of at least six months (primary) and at approximately three months (secondary). Exploratory sensitivity analyses were restricted to biochemically verified abstinence, and further analyses examined missing-data assumptions, completeness of AI reporting and results available only in trial registries. Certainty of evidence was assessed using GRADE. Results Fourteen RCTs involving 101,331 randomised participants were included, eight of which contributed to meta-analysis. AI functions comprised message recommender systems (five trials), conversational agents (three trials), wearable-sensor smoking-detection models (three trials), lapse-risk prediction models applied to ecological momentary assessments (two trials) and one app described as AI-enabled without technical detail. Pooled abstinence at six months or longer was RR 1.33 (95 % CI 0.82-2.15; I-squared = 67.6 %; four trials, 2,694 participants), and at approximately three months RR 1.36 (95 % CI 0.63-2.93; I-squared = 58.4 %; four trials, 715 participants). Exploratory analyses restricted to biochemically verified abstinence yielded RR 1.53 (95 % CI 1.07-2.19; three trials, 1,207 participants) at six months or longer and RR 2.03 (95 % CI 1.03-4.03; three trials, 366 participants) at approximately three months; these analyses changed the composition of the evidence set by excluding the largest null trials and should not be interpreted as confirmatory. Adding two completed trials whose results were available only in a trial registry moved the six-month estimate towards the null (RR 1.20, 95 % CI 0.91-1.59). In an exploratory comparison by comparator architecture, point estimates more consistently favoured AI-enabled packages versus usual or minimal care than versus active non-AI digital comparators, where results were inconsistent; however, comparator type was confounded with other trial characteristics. Certainty of evidence ranged from low to very low. No included trial randomised a generative large language model intervention. Conclusions Randomised evidence for AI-enabled smoking cessation remains sparse, heterogeneous and imprecise. AI-containing packages may improve abstinence when added to usual or minimal care, but current trials do not establish a consistent incremental benefit of AI over well-designed non-AI digital support. Larger trials with biochemically verified long-term endpoints, matched comparators that isolate the algorithmic contribution, and transparent AI-specific reporting are needed before superiority of AI-enabled cessation support can be inferred.

titre: Forecasting Next-Day Alcohol Craving in Individuals With Problematic Alcohol Use With Multimodal Data and a Tiny Recurrent Neural Network: Prospective Longitudinal Study.
auteurs: Lee D, Lee JY, Lee H, Kwon M, Song S, Yoon J, Jung YC, Ahn WY, Choi JS.
resume: Background Alcohol craving is associated with drinking behaviors despite negative consequences and relapse following periods of abstinence or treatment. Accurately forecasting alcohol craving is crucial for preventing alcohol consumption and relapse, thereby mitigating alcohol-related problems. Previous studies have assessed alcohol craving using diverse modalities such as psychological assessments, neurophysiological measures including electroencephalography (EEG) or heart rate variability (HRV) at a single time point, and digital phenotypes collected longitudinally via smartphone apps. However, alcohol craving is inherently heterogeneous and multidimensional across individuals and over time, making it difficult to capture using any single modality alone. In contrast, multimodal AI enables the prediction of alcohol craving by integrating complementary behavioral and neurophysiological features. Objective This study aimed to develop and evaluate AI models to forecast next-day alcohol craving in individuals with problematic alcohol use with multimodal datasets. Methods We analyzed multimodal datasets comprising smartphone-based digital phenotypes collected over 28 days, along with baseline EEG, HRV, and psychological measures in a prospective longitudinal study of 60 participants with problematic alcohol use. A tiny multimodal recurrent neural network (RNN) was implemented, in which representations of static baseline features were encoded into a latent representation and used to initialize the hidden state of the RNN. Model performance was evaluated using accuracy, weighted F 1 -score, macro F 1 -score, and mean absolute error (MAE). Results The multimodal model consistently outperformed the unimodal model based on digital phenotypes alone, achieving higher accuracy (0.56 vs 0.45), weighted F 1 -score (0.51 vs 0.38), and macro F 1 -score (0.37 vs 0.24), along with lower MAE (0.68 vs 0.90). At the individual level, 72% (43/60) of participants showed improved prediction accuracy with the multimodal model. These improvements were statistically significant (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, P t test, P Conclusions Integrating digital phenotypes with neurophysiological and psychological features enhances the prediction of short-term alcohol craving dynamics. This approach may enable more precise and timely personalized interventions for individuals at risk of relapse.
